extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of literature, culture, and moral criticism (educated general public)
extracted.subtask_description: Critical-essay prose articulating what 'culture' is, its proper motives and functions, and how to judge social institutions and values by a standard of human perfection. Aims to give evaluative principles for culture versus mere machinery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Culture as the study of perfection
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture is properly described as having its origin in the love of perfection; it is a study of perfection — not merely a desire to see things as they are but an endeavour to make reason and the will of God prevail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arnold contrasts a narrow curiosity-driven 'culture' with this broader view: culture's chief aim is the pursuit and propagation of human perfection, conceived as inward, harmonious growth ('not a having and a resting, but a growing and a becoming'). Culture should therefore prepare the way for improvements in institutions and conduct by informing what ought to be done.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right motives for culture: scientific curiosity vs social passion
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two motives of culture: (a) the scientific passion — desire to see things as they are (curiosity in a praiseworthy sense); (b) the social/moral passion — the love of perfection and desire to do good. Genuine culture combines both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish laudable curiosity (Montesquieu: 'To render an intelligent being yet more intelligent!') from mere frivolous curiosity; avoid culture that is only exclusiveness, vanity, or class distinction. Culture should not be merely speculative but informed by a moral passion to reduce human error and misery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of thought and action
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture is marked by combining the scientific passion (thinking) with the passion for doing good (acting); it is not primarily bent on immediate action but on ensuring action is based on reason and right principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arnold warns against the social passion becoming overhasty and substituting crude conceptions for reason; culture's role is to remember that 'acting and instituting are of little use, unless we know how and what we ought to act and to institute.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Inward condition over external machinery
rubrics_metrics.description: Human perfection consists in an inward condition of mind and spirit, not in outward circumstances; wealth, machinery, population, railroads, and similar external goods are 'machinery,' not ends in themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate institutions and national success by spiritual and aesthetic standards, not merely material indicators (e.g., coal or wealth). Culture's task is to 'purge' minds of the delusion that such external things constitute greatness and to set true standards of perfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: General expansion and social obligation
rubrics_metrics.description: Perfection, as culture conceives it, must be general — the individual cannot be perfected in isolation; the individual is 'obliged... to carry others along with him in his march towards perfection.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultural judgments should favor growth that benefits the human community at large; culture imposes a duty to promote the 'kingdom of God' (happiness) by increasing others' welfare, not only one's own.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmonious development of faculties
rubrics_metrics.description: Perfection requires a harmonious expansion of all human powers; it is not consistent with the over-development of any one power at the expense of the rest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique tendencies that overvalue a single capacity (e.g., mere moral energy without aesthetic sense, or purely intellectual attainment without moral fibre). The ideal unites beauty and intelligence ('sweetness and light').

rubrics_metrics.name: Sweetness and light as cultural criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture's characteristic qualities are 'sweetness and light' — beauty and intelligence; these are the marks by which cultural achievement and humane character should be judged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arnold points to Greek achievements as exemplifying this combination and urges modern society to restore attention to beauty and harmony alongside moral strength. Use 'sweetness and light' to test literature, manners, and institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of worshipping machinery (wealth, population, health) as ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not treat wealth, population, bodily health, or technological development as final proofs of greatness; when pursued as ends they vulgarise life and are signs of Philistinism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess social ideals by asking whether the lives they produce are attractive and humane; culture generates 'dissatisfaction' with mere material aims and thereby resists vulgarisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use culture to test and criticise religious organisations
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture, like poetry, applies an ideal of complete human perfection to judge religious organisations; it can recognise the good they do while exposing the narrowness of their ideal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let pious language mask inadequate standards. Evaluate religious bodies by the fullness of the life they encourage (do they cultivate sweetness and light and a rounded human nature?), not merely by their moral strictness or institutional success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discipline: sincerity, earnestness, and practice
rubrics_metrics.description: From Hebraism: the discipline of walking staunchly by the best light one has — being strict and sincere with oneself, not being of those 'who say and do not,' and being in earnest — is essential for ennobling life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate persons and institutions by their sincerity and capacity to translate knowledge into action. Arnold praises Hebraic energy of faith ('If ye know these things, happy are ye if ye do them!') as necessary to make ideals effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Culture's practical role: dissipate delusions and fix real standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture's function is to dissipate delusions about what constitutes greatness and to fix real standards of perfection that are spiritual and aesthetic rather than mechanical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical cultural work includes educating tastes (getting 'the raw person to like' the truly beautiful and becoming), resisting false complacency about national greatness, and defending the long-term preservation of humane values in an industrial society.
